{{Nihongo|'''Shuji Nakamura'''|中村 修二|Nakamura Shūji|born May 22, 1954}} is a Japanese–American [[electrical engineer]] and co-inventor of the [[Light-emitting diode#Blue LED|blue LED]], a major breakthrough in lighting technology.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pacbiztimes.com/2014/10/10/laureate-fought-the-odds-to-make-history |title=Nobel laureate fought the odds to make history|date=10 October 2014 |access-date=Oct 10, 2014|publisher=Pacific Coast Business Times}}</ref> For this achievement, Nakamura, together with [[Isamu Akasaki]] and [[Hiroshi Amano]], received the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] in 2014.<ref name="Nobel Prize">{{Cite web|title=Nobel Prize in Physics 2014|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2014/summary/|url-status=live|publisher=NobelPrize.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240407181951/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2014/summary/|archive-date=2024-04-07|access-date=2014-10-07}}</ref>

Nakamura specializes in the field of [[semiconductor]] technology. He is Professor of Materials and of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] (UCSB) since 1999.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.engr.ucsb.edu/faculty/profile/82|title=Shuji Nakamura|access-date=July 31, 2008|publisher=University of California, Santa Barbara|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100715103346/http://www1.engr.ucsb.edu/faculty/profile/82|archive-date=July 15, 2010}}</ref>

== Career and research ==
Shuji Nakamura was born on May 22, 1954, in [[Ikata]], [[Ehime Prefecture]], Japan.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Shuji Nakamura, Ph.D.|url=https://www.horiba.com/int/scientific/resources/nobel-laureate-connections/shuji-nakamura-phd/|publisher=Horiba|access-date=October 18, 2026}}</ref> In 1973, he entered the [[University of Tokushima]], where he received his [[Bachelor of Engineering]] and [[Master of Science]] degrees in Electrical Engineering in 1977 and 1979, respectively. Nakamura joined the [[Nichia Corporation]] in 1979, also based in [[Tokushima]].<ref name="Nobel bio"/><ref name="UCSB">{{Cite web|title=Short Bio|url=https://ssleec.ucsb.edu/nakamura|publisher=University of California, Santa Barbara|access-date=October 18, 2026}}</ref> It was while working for Nichia that Nakamura invented the method for producing the first commercial high brightness [[gallium nitride]] (GaN) LED whose brilliant blue light, when partially converted to yellow by a phosphor coating, is the key to white LED lighting, which went into production in 1993.

Previously, J.&nbsp;I. Pankove and co-workers at [[RCA Corporation|RCA]] put in considerable effort but did not make a marketable GaN LED in the 1960s. The principal problem was the difficulty of making strongly [[Extrinsic semiconductor#P-type semiconductors|p-type]] GaN.{{sfnp|Johnstone|2007|pp=90–93}} Nakamura drew on the work of another Japanese group led by Professor [[Isamu Akasaki]], who published their method to make strongly p-type GaN by electron-beam irradiation of magnesium-doped GaN; however, this method was not suitable for mass production. Nakamura developed a thermal annealing method much more suitable for mass production.{{sfnp|Johnstone|2007|p=114}} In addition, he and his co-workers worked out the physics and pointed out the culprit was hydrogen, which passivated acceptors in GaN.{{sfnp|Johnstone|2007|pp=114, 116}}

At the time, many considered creating a GaN LED too difficult to produce; therefore, Nakamura was fortunate that the founder of Nichia, {{interlanguage link|Nobuo Ogawa|ja| 小川信雄 (実業家)}} (1912–2002), was willing to support and fund his GaN project.<ref name=normile/>{{sfnp|Johnstone|2007|p=68}} However, the senior Ogawa ceded the presidency to his son-in-law Eiji Ogawa (in 1989). The company under Eiji's direction ordered him to suspend work on GaN, claiming it was consuming too much time and money.{{sfnp|Johnstone|2007|pp=103–104}}<ref name=jt20020920/> Nakamura continued to develop the blue LED on his own and in 1993 succeeded in making the device.{{sfnp|Johnstone|2007|pp=112–120}}<ref name=jt20020920/>

Despite these circumstances, once Nakamura succeeded in creating a commercially viable prototype, 3 orders of magnitude (1000 times) brighter than previously successful blue LEDs, Nichia pursued developing the marketable product.<ref name=normile/>{{sfnp|Johnstone|2007|pp=120–121}} The company's gross receipt surged from just over ¥20 billion (≈US$200 million) in 1993 to ¥80 billion (≈US$800 million) by 2001, 60 percent of which was accounted for by sales of blue LED products.<ref name=jt20020920/> The company's workforce doubled between 1994 and 1999 from 640 to 1300 employees.{{sfnp|Johnstone|2007|p=122}} 

In 1994, the University of Tokushima conferred Nakamura a [[Doctor of Philosophy by publication]].<ref name="UCSB"/><ref name="Nobel bio">[https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2014/nakamura/biographical/ Shuji Nakamura – Biographical] - website of the Nobel Prize</ref>

Nakamura left Nichia Corporation in 1999 to join the faculty at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] at the personal invitation of the university's chancellor, [[Henry T. Yang]]. Yang flew three times from California to Japan to recruit Nakamura, with promises to build new research facilities and having a Japanese-speaking research staff team already assembled for him.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=美国加州大学圣巴巴拉分校校长杨祖佑：寻找天才为大师建大楼 |url=https://www.cas.cn/xw/kjsm/gjdt/200906/t20090608_635081.shtml |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250627221639/https://www.cas.cn/xw/kjsm/gjdt/200906/t20090608_635081.shtml |archive-date=2025-06-27 |access-date=2025-06-27 |website=Chinese Academy of Sciences}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=美国加州大学圣塔巴巴拉分校校长杨祖佑："一流教授最看重和谐科研环境" - 中华人民共和国教育部 |url=http://www.moe.gov.cn/jyb_xwfb/xw_zt/moe_357/s3579/moe_1217/moe_1218/tnull_16562.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250627221708/http://www.moe.gov.cn/jyb_xwfb/xw_zt/moe_357/s3579/moe_1217/moe_1218/tnull_16562.html |archive-date=2025-06-27 |access-date=2025-06-27 |website=Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China}}</ref>

In 2001, Nakamura sued his former employer Nichia over his bonus for the discovery as a part of a series of lawsuits between Nichia and Nakamura with Nichia's US competitor [[Cree Inc.]]; they agreed in 2000 to jointly sue Nichia at the expense of Cree and Nakamura received stock options from Cree. Nakamura claimed that he received only {{JP¥|20,000|link=yes}} (≈{{US$|180|link=yes}}) for his discovery of "404 patent," though Nichia's president Eiji Ogawa's side of the story was that he was shocked beyond belief that the court would award Nakamura ¥20 billion, and downplaying the significance of the "404 patent," opined that the company had adequately compensated him for the innovation through promotions and bonuses amounting to ¥62 million over 11 years and annual salary which was raised to ¥20 million by the time Nakamura quit Nichia.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nichia kagaku kōgyō no Ogawa Eiji shi: soshō sōdō no shinjitsu wo ima koso akiraka ni suru |script-title=ja:日亜化学工業社長の小川英治氏 訴訟騒動の真実を今こそ明らかにする |trans-title=Nichia president Eiji Ogawa [says] I am now going to clarify the truth behind the lawsuit <!--Series: 食い違うそれぞれの「真実」 日亜化学工業社長と中村氏/「青色LED訴訟」の深層 The conflicting 'truths' [from] Nichia and Mr. Nakamura, the deeper side of the Blue LED lawsuit-->|publisher=Nikkei Tech-on |url=http://techon.nikkeibp.co.jp/NEWS/nakamura/mono200404_2.html |language=ja |date=April 2004 |access-date=1 December 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141007160518/http://techon.nikkeibp.co.jp/NEWS/nakamura/mono200404_2.html |archive-date=7 October 2014}}</ref>

Nakamura sued for ¥2 billion (<US$20 million) as his fair share for the invention, and the district court awarded him ten times the amount, ¥20 billion (<US$200 million). However, Nichia appealed the award and the parties settled in 2005 for ¥840 million (≈US$8.1 million, less than 5% of the award amount), which was still the largest payment ever paid by a Japanese company to an employee for an invention,<ref>{{cite news|last=Zaun |first=Todd |date=January 12, 2005 |title=Japanese Company to Pay Ex-Employee $8.1 Million for Invention |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/01/12/business/worldbusiness/12light.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=October 7, 2014}}</ref>{{sfnp|Johnstone|2007|pp=233–237}} an amount only enough to cover legal expenses incurred by Nakamura.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ft.com/content/d4f26220-e1ec-11db-af9e-000b5df10621|title=Book Review: The man who had the world's brightest idea |author=Robert Matthews |publisher=Financial Times |date=3 April 2007 |access-date=6 April 2021}}</ref> In line with the lawsuit, Nakamura has repeatedly criticized Japanese companies for not giving their researchers the salaries and recognition they deserve.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Japanese Inventor Sues Company |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/japanese-inventor-sues-company#:~:text=Since%20leaving%20Nichia%20for%20the,reasonable%20compensation,%22%20he%20says |access-date=2025-05-19 |website=www.science.org |language=en}}</ref>

Nakamura has also worked on green LEDs and is responsible for creating the white LED and [[blue laser]] diodes used in [[Blu-ray Disc]]s and [[HD DVD]]s.<ref>{{cite news|date=June 15, 2006|url= https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=5488821|title=Work in Colored Lights Nets Millennium Prize|author=Richard Harris|work=[[All Things Considered]]}}</ref>

Nakamura is a professor of Materials at the UCSB.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sslec.ucsb.edu/nakamura/|title=Shuji Nakamura|access-date=October 19, 2012|publisher=Solid State Lighting & Energy Center|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130528163504/http://sslec.ucsb.edu/nakamura/|archive-date=May 28, 2013}}</ref> In 2008, Nakamura, along with fellow UCSB professors Dr. [[Steven P. DenBaars]] and Dr. James Speck, founded Soraa, a developer of solid-state lighting technology built on pure gallium nitride substrates.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.soraa.com/about|title=About|access-date=October 19, 2012|publisher=Soraa Inc.}}</ref> Nakamura holds 208 US utility patents as of 5 May 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&u=%2Fnetahtml%2FPTO%2Fsearch-adv.htm&r=0&p=1&f=S&l=50&d=PTXT&Query=apt%2F1+and+in%2FNakamura-Shuji+and+an%2F%28%22university+of+california%22+or+nichia+or+cree+or+soraa%29 |title=Patents of Shuji Nakamura |access-date=2020-05-03 |archive-date=2021-04-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210402091341/http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&u=/netahtml/PTO/search-adv.htm&r=0&p=1&f=S&l=50&d=PTXT&Query=apt/1+and+in/Nakamura-Shuji+and+an/%28%22university+of+california%22+or+nichia+or+cree+or+soraa%29 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In November 2022, Nakamura co-founded a [[List of nuclear fusion companies|commercial fusion company, Blue Laser Fusion]], with Hiroaki Ohta, a former president of Tokyo-based drone maker ACSL.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Nuclear fusion race draws in Nobel-winning LED pioneer |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Energy/Nuclear-fusion-race-draws-in-Nobel-winning-LED-pioneer |access-date=July 25, 2023 |website=NIKKEI Asia |publication-date=July 23, 2023}}</ref> In July 2023, Blue Laser Fusion raised $25 million from venture capital firm [[JAFCO]] Group and the Mirai Creation Fund, which is backed by [[Toyota]] Motor and other investors and managed by the [[SPARX Group]].<ref name=":0"/>

== Personal life ==
Nakamura is married to Yuki Nakamura.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-12-11 |title=Japanese Nobel physics laureate Shuji Nakamura and his spouse Yuki... |url=https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/japanese-nobel-physics-laureate-shuji-nakamura-and-his-news-photo/460318898 |access-date=2024-03-10 |website=Getty Images |language=en-us}}</ref>
